Graph theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Foundations of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 68k Articles: 883
Graph theory studies vertices and the edges connecting them: which graph paths exist, how efficiently we can travel, and which connections are indispensable. A road map becomes a graph when junctions are vertices and road segments are edges; a communications network uses routers and links instead. The drawing helps us see connections, but its apparent lengths need not be the costs being optimized. Record travel times or transmission costs separately in a weighted graph.
The appeal of graph theory is that one model serves many practical questions. Graph paths describe routes, connected components of a graph identify isolated regions, and minimum spanning trees connect all locations cheaply. The shortest path problem asks a different question: find the cheapest journey between specified locations. Our four-vertex example below makes that distinction concrete and shows how the Dijkstra algorithm discovers a route without trying every graph path.

Path-cycle matching

Words: 65
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A path-cycle matching in a finite simple graph is a collection of mutually vertex-disjoint paths and cycles in a graph. Its used edges form a subgraph with every degree of a vertex at most two. Conversely, every finite connected component of a graph with maximum degree at most two is a graph path, a cycle in a graph, or an isolated vertex; following successive edges proves this classification. Discarding unused isolated vertices therefore converts any such subgraph into a path-cycle matching without changing its edge count. On a bipartite graph, maximizing the used edges is exactly bipartite b-matching with every bv​=2.

Tree decomposition ((T,(Bt​)t∈V(T)​))

Words: 111 Articles: 1
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A tree of bags of graph vertices such that every vertex occurs in a bag, both endpoints of every graph edge occur together in a bag, and the bags containing any fixed vertex form a connected connected subgraph of a tree. Its width is maxt​∣Bt​∣−1. The connected-occurrence condition lets subproblems agree on shared variables while solving a constraint satisfaction problem; an arbitrary cover of edges by small bags is insufficient.

Treewidth (tw(G)=minT​(maxB∈T​∣B∣−1))

Words: 55
Tree decomposition OurBigBook.com
The minimum width of a tree decomposition. A tree has width at most one, while a clique of k vertices forces width at least k−1. Every pair of vertices in the clique shares a bag; their connected bag connected subgraphs of a tree have a common intersection by the Helly property of connected connected subgraphs of a tree, placing the whole clique in one bag. Small treewidth is useful for dynamic programming on finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems.

K-core peeling invariant

Words: 69
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
During repeated deletion of vertices of current degree below k, every subgraph of minimum degree at least k is contained in the active induced subgraph. If an active vertex has degree below k, its degree in any subgraph of the active graph is no greater, so no candidate can contain it. This proves the invariant inductively. A queue of threshold crossings and adjacency lists implements peeling in O(∣V∣+∣E∣) time.

K-core (Ck​(G))

Words: 48
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The unique maximal induced subgraph with minimum vertex degree at least k, possibly empty. It is found by repeatedly deleting vertices of degree below k. The k-core peeling invariant proves that every subgraph satisfying that degree bound survives inside the result; in particular the final vertex set does not depend on deletion order.

Dominating set (V=D∪⋃v∈D​N(v))

Words: 46
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A dominating set D of a graph is a vertex subset such that every unselected vertex has a neighbour in D. Equivalently every vertex lies in D or is adjacent to an element of D. This condition differs from vertex cover, which requires every edge to have an endpoint in the selected set.

Edge cover (F⊆E,⋃e∈F​e=V)

Words: 81 Articles: 1
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
An edge cover of a finite graph is a subset of its edges incident to every vertex. It exists if and only if there is no isolated vertex, with the empty graph covered by the empty set. A minimum-cardinality edge cover uses as few edges as possible; a minimum-weight edge cover minimizes their total weight. These objectives are related to maximum cardinality matching and maximum-weight matching, respectively, by the edge cover and matching identity and minimum-weight edge cover by matching savings.

Minimum-weight edge cover

Words: 26
Edge cover OurBigBook.com
An edge cover minimizing the sum of selected edge weights. For nonnegative weights and no isolated vertex, it is computable in polynomial time by the minimum-weight edge cover by matching savings construction. It need not have minimum cardinality.

Network robustness

Words: 83 Articles: 3
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Persistence of a specified network property under a specified class of perturbations. Robustness of connectivity and robustness of dynamical function are different questions.

Network redundancy

Words: 19
Network robustness OurBigBook.com
Alternative routes or components can preserve function after failure, provided they do not share the same relevant failure mode.

Network resilience

Words: 41 Articles: 1
Network robustness OurBigBook.com
Maintenance or recovery of specified network performance after a disturbance, including its transient response and recovery time.

Cascading failure

Words: 24
Network resilience OurBigBook.com
A failure changes loads or dependencies so that further components fail. Connectivity of the surviving graph alone does not determine whether a cascade occurs.

Network motif

Words: 34
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A small interaction pattern occurring unusually often relative to a specified network null model. A circuit's wiring and proposed dynamical function should be distinguished from the statistical evidence that its pattern is enriched in a network.

Community detection

Words: 35
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Community detection partitions a network into groups according to a specified structural criterion, often excess internal connectivity. The output depends on the objective, so a partition inferred from topology need not by itself establish distinct biological functions.

Network null model

Words: 43
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A network null model specifies the reference network ensemble or expected connectivity against which a pattern is measured. For standard network modularity, expected edge weight is ki​kj​/(2m). The reference is part of the scientific model: choosing a different reference can change what counts as excess structure.

Network modularity (Q=(2m)−1∑ij​(Aij​−ki​kj​/(2m))1{ci​=cj​})

Words: 43
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Network modularity measures excess within-community edge weight relative to a network null model based on degrees of vertices. For an undirected unweighted graph, its standard form is Q=(2m)−1∑ij​(Aij​−ki​kj​/(2m))1{ci​=cj​}. A single community containing every vertex has Q=0; a partition with more internal connectivity than expected can have positive Q.

Louvain method

Words: 40
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The Louvain method is a greedy multilevel community detection algorithm maximizing network modularity. It alternates positive-gain single-vertex moves with contraction of communities into weighted vertices. Different vertex orders can produce different local optima; a result is not a certificate of globally maximum modularity.[ref]

Eigenvector centrality (Av=λmax​v)

Words: 42
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Eigenvector centrality assigns nonnegative vertex scores proportional to the sum of neighbouring scores: vi​=λmax−1​∑j​Aij​vj​. It uses a nonnegative eigenvector of the adjacency matrix for its largest positive eigenvalue. State the normalization, such as Euclidean norm one. For a three-leaf star graph, hub and leaf scores have ratio 3​.

Degree-preserving edge rewiring

Words: 48
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Degree-preserving edge rewiring replaces two edges (u,v) and (x,y) by (u,y) and (x,v), preserving every endpoint's degree of a vertex. On simple graphs, reject proposed self-loops and duplicate edges. Symmetric random proposals with rejected moves retained preserve a uniform distribution on the reachable realizations; adequate mixing remains a separate requirement. Connectivity can change unless explicitly constrained.

Scale-free network (P(k)∝k−γ)

Words: 35
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A scale-free network has a degree distribution with an approximately power-law tail over a meaningful range. Evidence requires degrees from enough vertices to assess that range and compare alternative tail models. Large clustering coefficients or short graph distances alone do not establish this property.

Degree distribution (P(k))

Words: 30
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A degree distribution assigns the fraction or probability of vertices having each degree of a vertex. For an observed network, P(k)=#{i:ki​=k}/n. Preserving every labelled degree preserves this distribution, but preserving only its mean does not.

Small-worldness (σ=(C/Crand​)/(L/Lrand​))

Words: 41
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Small-worldness compares a network's clustering and average shortest-path length to reference values through σ=(C/Crand​)/(L/Lrand​). The common σ>1 classification is a ratio-based convention rather than a significance test; random-reference variability must be assessed separately.[ref]

Small-world network

Words: 36
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A small-world network combines elevated local clustering coefficients with mean graph distance comparable to a chosen reference ensemble of random graphs. Both the reference ensemble and the clustering convention must be specified. A network can have these properties without having a power-law degree distribution.

Clustering coefficient (Ci​=2ei​/[ki​(ki​−1)])

Words: 56
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
For a vertex with ki​≥2 neighbours in a simple graph, its local clustering coefficient is Ci​=ei​/(2ki​​), where ei​ counts edges among those neighbours. It is the fraction of possible neighbour-neighbour edges that are present. A common network summary averages these local coefficients, setting them to zero for degrees below two; this differs from weighting by the number of neighbour pairs.

Spanning forest

Words: 27
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
An acyclic spanning subgraph containing a spanning tree of each connected component of the original graph. For a graph with n vertices and c components, a spanning forest has n−c edges.

Circle graph

Words: 96 Articles: 2
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The intersection graph of chords of a circle: each chord is a vertex, and two vertices are adjacent when their chords cross. Two chords with distinct endpoints cross exactly when their endpoints alternate around the circle.

Permutation graph

Words: 62 Articles: 1
Circle graph OurBigBook.com
The intersection graph of the segments in a permutation diagram. Two segments cross exactly when their endpoint orders disagree. A set of mutually noncrossing segments corresponds to a monotone subsequence of the endpoint permutation.

Permutation diagram

Words: 31
Permutation graph OurBigBook.com
A diagram of straight segments joining two parallel lines, with distinct endpoints on each line. Ordering the endpoints along the two lines encodes a permutation; crossing segments define the associated permutation graph.

Graph bandwidth

Graph theory OurBigBook.com

Interval graph

Graph theory OurBigBook.com

Pathwidth

Graph theory OurBigBook.com

Chip-firing game

Words: 57 Articles: 1
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A discrete process in which a vertex holding at least its degree in chips may send one chip along each incident edge. On the infinite line, a firing removes two chips from a site and gives one to each neighbor. When stabilization exists, commuting local firings explain why their order does not change the final stable configuration.

Abelian sandpile model

Chip-firing game OurBigBook.com

De Bruijn graph

Words: 53
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
For an alphabet of size q, the order-n directed graph has words of length n−1 as vertices and words of length n as edges. An edge goes from its prefix of length n−1 to its suffix of that length. An Eulerian cycle therefore lists every length-n word once as a cyclic window, producing a De Bruijn sequence.

Geometric spanner (dG​(u,v)≤t∥u−v∥)

Words: 90
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A geometric spanner is a weighted graph on points in Euclidean space, with edge weights equal to their Euclidean distances, in which every pair has a graph path of length at most t times its direct distance. Its stretch factor is the largest ratio dG​(u,v)/∥u−v∥, where dG​ is shortest-path distance. A square's four perimeter edges, without diagonals, give stretch factor 2​: adjacent points have ratio one, and diagonal pairs have route length 2 instead of 2​. The aim is to retain short routes with fewer edges than a complete graph. [ref].

Graph excess (exc(G)=∣E(G)∣−∣V(G)∣)

Words: 253 Articles: 3
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Here excess means edges minus vertices. For a connected graph it is one less than the number of independent cycles. Deleting a leaf and its incident edge, or suppressing a degree-two vertex, preserves excess. This convention differs by one from the cyclomatic number for connected graphs.

Bicyclic graph (∣E∣=∣V∣+1)

Words: 209 Articles: 2
Graph excess OurBigBook.com
A connected bicyclic graph has two independent cycles, equivalently excess one. Its 2-core has the same excess and every removed vertex lies in a tree attached to the core. The graph kernel captures the finite collection of possible branching structures.

Labelled bicyclic graph count (C(n,n+1)=Θ(nn+1)(n≥4))

Words: 95
Bicyclic graph OurBigBook.com
If bk​ counts labelled bicyclic cores on k vertices, the bicyclic kernel classification gives bk​≤Ak!k2. Three internally nonempty paths between two branching vertices give bk​≥k!(2k−3​)/12 for k≥5. Attach a forest with those core vertices as roots to obtain C(n,n+1)=∑k​(kn​)bk​knn−k−1. After division by nn+1 the relevant sum is n−2∑k​k3(n)k​/nk. Its upper bound follows from (n)k​/nk≤e−k(k−1)/(2n); its lower bound uses n​≤k≤2n​, where this product stays bounded below. The sum is bounded above and below by positive constants. The restriction n≥4 is necessary: C(3,4)=0.

Bicyclic kernel classification

Words: 77
Bicyclic graph OurBigBook.com
The graph kernel of a bicyclic graph satisfies ∑v​(degv−2)=2, with all degrees at least three. It therefore has either one degree-four vertex carrying two loops, a bouquet graph, or two degree-three vertices. In the latter case connectivity and degree counting give either three parallel edges, the three-edge Theta graph, or one edge between the vertices and one loop at each, a dumbbell graph. All bicyclic cores are subdivisions of these three kernels, subject to simplicity restrictions on loop lengths and parallel paths.

2-core of a graph (C2​(G))

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The 2-core is what remains of a finite simple graph after repeatedly removing every vertex with fewer than two surviving graph neighbours. It strips away dangling trees while keeping the part that can support itself under this local rule. Precisely, for an undirected graph G=(V,E), its 2-core is the unique maximum by set inclusion induced subgraph G[S] such that
degG[S]​(v)≥2for every v∈S.
(1)
The empty vertex set is allowed: the condition is then vacuous, without needing to define the minimum degree of the empty graph. "Maximum by inclusion" means that S contains every other vertex set satisfying the condition. It is stronger than merely saying that one chosen set cannot be enlarged: the 2-core simultaneously contains all possible qualifying induced subgraphs. In this particular family, every inclusion-maximal qualifying set does equal that unique maximum; the union argument in why the 2-core is unique explains why. [ref]
For a complete worked example, let ab denote the edge {a,b} and take
V={a,b,c,d,e,f,g,z},E={ab,bc,ca,cd,de,ef,dg}.
(2)
The triangle in a graph abc has a branching tail attached at c, and z is an isolated vertex. In alphabetical order the initial degrees of vertices are (2,2,3,3,2,1,1,0). Deleting f turns e into a leaf of a graph; deleting g leaves d with degree of a vertex two; deleting z changes no other degree of a vertex. Now delete e, which makes d a leaf of a graph, and finally delete d. Exactly the three edges of abc remain: C2​(G)=G[{a,b,c}].
A forest has empty 2-core: every nonempty finite forest has an isolated vertex or a leaf of a graph, so deletion cannot stop at a nonempty remainder. In particular, an isolated edge, an isolated vertex, a path graph, and the empty graph all have empty 2-core. Every cycle graph is its own 2-core. Two disjoint triangles in a graph also form their own 2-core, so a 2-core need not be a connected graph; attaching a tree to either triangle changes neither surviving triangle.

Leaf pruning for the 2-core

Words: 236
2-core of a graph OurBigBook.com
Use adjacency lists and a FIFO queue to implement the deletion rule in time complexity O(∣V∣+∣E∣). Compute each initial degree of a vertex once, mark every vertex alive, and put all vertices of degree of a vertex zero or one in the FIFO queue. Each vertex is inserted at most once. Repeatedly remove the front vertex v, mark it dead, and traverse its original adjacency list. For each still-alive graph neighbour u, decrease the stored degree of a vertex of u by one; if it has just become one, append u. A vertex already queued can drop from one to zero before its turn, but it stays queued and requires no second insertion. Stop when the FIFO queue is empty; the alive vertices induce C2​(G).
For the displayed example, initially enqueue (f,g,z) in that order. The successive FIFO queues, after each deletion and all its updates, are
(f,g,z)−f​(g,z,e)−g​(z,e)−z​(e)−e​(d)−d​().
(3)
This explains the delayed deletion of d: its initial degree of a vertex was three, but the relevant degree of a vertex is always its current one in the surviving induced subgraph. Removing only the original vertices of degree of a vertex one would give the wrong answer.
Initialization inspects every vertex and every adjacency list entry once. During deletion each original adjacency list is traversed at most once, so at most 2∣E∣ entries are inspected in an undirected graph. All insertions, removals and stored-degree updates cost constant time each. Thus total time complexity is O(∣V∣+∣E∣) and additional storage, beyond the adjacency lists, is O(∣V∣). The cost includes isolated vertices; repeatedly rescanning the whole surviving graph after each deletion would lose this bound. The single-threshold FIFO queue method is enough for the 2-core; the full k-core of a graph decomposition computes all thresholds.

Why the 2-core is unique

Words: 155
2-core of a graph OurBigBook.com
Suppose T is any vertex set whose induced subgraph has every degree of a vertex at least two. No vertex of T can be the first one deleted from T: before such a deletion it still has its two graph neighbours within T, contradicting eligibility for deletion. Consequently every qualifying T survives every legal deletion sequence. Once deletion stops, its remainder R itself qualifies, because every surviving vertex has at least two surviving graph neighbours. Therefore T⊆R for every qualifying T: G[R] is the unique maximum and the final remainder is independent of deletion order. The intermediate FIFO queues and deletion orders can differ.
There is also a direct existence argument. If A and B qualify, then A∪B qualifies: each vertex retains at least the two graph neighbours it already had in A or in B. Taking the union of all qualifying vertex sets produces the maximum. This rules out a collection of competing, incomparable inclusion-maximal answers. It also explains why restricting the search to connected subgraphs would change the question.

Bridges and connectivity in the 2-core

Words: 304
2-core of a graph OurBigBook.com
A 2-core can contain bridges in a graph, and even vertices that lie on no cycle in a graph. Consider the dumbbell graph, also called a barbell in this example, made of two disjoint triangles in a graph joined by a graph path with two internal vertices:
V={a,b,c,x,y,d,e,f},E={ab,bc,ca,cx,xy,yd,de,ef,fd}.
(4)
Here c,d have degree of a vertex three, and every other vertex has degree of a vertex two. No deletion is possible, so the whole graph is its 2-core. Yet cx,xy,yd are bridges in a graph: deleting any one separates the two triangles. None belongs to a cycle in a graph, and x,y belong to no cycle in a graph either. Keeping only edges on graph cycles would incorrectly discard the entire joining graph path.
Every cycle in a graph does survive pruning, because each of its vertices keeps its two cycle graph neighbours. The barbell shows that the converse fails: the 2-core can be larger than the union of all graph cycles. Its condition is local minimum degree, not protection against a single connection failing.
A biconnected component is a different object: a maximal connected subgraph with no cut vertex of its own. Under the block convention used here, the barbell has five biconnected components: its two triangles and its three individual joining edges, each with its endpoints. Its cut vertices are c,x,y,d. A 2-connected component with at least three vertices must remain connected after any single vertex is deleted; the whole barbell fails that test. An informal phrase such as "biconnected core" therefore needs its own definition and must not be substituted for 2-core. Even an isolated edge is a block under this convention, although its 2-core is empty.
The usefulness of the 2-core is this precise separation of local persistence from global robustness. In a connected graph with nonempty 2-core, the deleted vertices form a forest, with each of its connected components of a graph attached by exactly one edge to the 2-core. Otherwise a deleted graph cycle, or a graph path joining two surviving attachment points, would itself have survived. Stripping these attached trees exposes a smaller structure for studying graph cycles, graph excess and the graph kernel, while preserving the joining bridges in a graph that organize that structure.

Graph kernel (K(G))

Words: 135
2-core of a graph OurBigBook.com
For a connected graph whose 2-core contains a vertex of degree of a vertex at least three, suppress each maximal graph path with degree-two internal vertices to a single edge, allowing its two endpoints to coincide. Here suppression is the reverse of graph subdivision. The resulting multigraph, retaining self-loops and parallel edges, is its graph kernel. Each suppressed internal vertex removes one vertex and one edge, preserving graph excess; counting a self-loop twice toward degree of a vertex, every remaining vertex has degree of a vertex at least three. A purely cyclic 2-core is a separate unicyclic case: it has no branching vertex to anchor this construction.
For the barbell in bridges and connectivity in the 2-core, the graph kernel has two vertices c,d, one self-loop at each, and a single joining edge cd. Suppressing x,y contracts the joining graph path to that bridge in a graph; suppressing the two other vertices on each triangle turns the triangle into a self-loop. The graph excess stays 9−8=3−2=1. Thus forming a graph kernel compresses degree-two chains rather than deleting everything outside graph cycles.

k-core of a graph (Ck​(G))

Words: 103
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative integer k, the k-core of a graph is the unique maximum by set inclusion induced subgraph in which every degree of a vertex is at least k, allowing the empty graph. Repeatedly delete vertices whose current degree of a vertex is less than k. These induced subgraphs are nested: Ck+1​(G)⊆Ck​(G); the case k=2 is the 2-core. In their 2003 preprint, Vladimir Batagelj and Matjaž Zaveršnik give an algorithm for the entire core decomposition, using degree buckets and constant-time position updates. Their general bound is O(∣V∣+∣E∣); the title's O(m) form applies to connected graphs with at least two vertices, where m=∣E∣≥∣V∣−1. [ref]

Chordal graph

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A chordal graph is a finite simple graph with no induced cycle of length at least four. Equivalently, every cycle in a graph with at least four vertices has a chord: an edge joining two nonconsecutive vertices of that graph cycle. The word "induced" matters: the induced subgraph on the chosen vertices must contain exactly the cycle's edges, with no chords. Triangles are allowed. This definition concerns adjacency, independently of how the graph is drawn.
For the square cycle graph C4​, take vertex set {a,b,c,d} and set of edges {ab,bc,cd,da}, where ab abbreviates {a,b}. Its graph neighbourhoods are N(a)=N(c)={b,d} and N(b)=N(d)={a,c}. The square is an induced cycle, so C4​ is not a chordal graph. Add the single edge ac: now N(a)={b,c,d}, N(b)={a,c}, N(c)={a,b,d}, and N(d)={a,c}. The only possible four-vertex graph cycle has chord ac, so this new graph is a chordal graph. Its maximal cliques are exactly {a,b,c} and {a,c,d}.
Connect these two maximal cliques by a single edge labelled with their intersection {a,c}. The result is a junction tree, also called a clique tree: its nodes are maximal cliques, and the nodes containing any fixed original vertex induce a connected graph inside the tree. Here a,c occur in both nodes, while b,d each occur in just one. This is the running intersection property. More generally, a nonempty connected graph is a chordal graph exactly when its maximal cliques admit such a tree; a disconnected chordal graph can be represented by one such tree per connected component of a graph.[ref]
A chordal graph need not be a planar graph: the complete graph K5​ is a chordal graph, since every pair of distinct vertices is adjacent, but its ten edges violate the planar graph edge bound ∣E∣≤3∣V∣−6=9. Conversely, even a plane drawing whose bounded faces are triangles can hide an induced cycle: a wheel graph with a four-vertex rim and a central vertex joined to the whole rim still has the rim as an induced cycle. Adding chords to obtain a chordal graph is called triangulation of an undirected graph; this is an adjacency condition, rather than a requirement about planar faces.
Why is this structure useful? The maximal cliques collect local interactions, and the running intersection property makes their overlaps sufficient for consistent communication. For random variables xa​,xb​,xc​,xd​ with finite state sets, a probabilistic graphical model of the square-plus-diagonal form can have
p(xa​,xb​,xc​,xd​)=Z−1ψabc​(xa​,xb​,xc​)ψacd​(xa​,xc​,xd​),
(5)
where the two nonnegative clique potentials have a positive normalizing constant Z. Eliminating xb​ produces the two-variable junction-tree sum-product message
m(xa​,xc​)=∑xb​​ψabc​(xa​,xb​,xc​),Z=∑xa​,xc​,xd​​m(xa​,xc​)ψacd​(xa​,xc​,xd​).
(6)
The shared clique {a,c} carries everything needed from the eliminated side. For q possible states per random variable, this example uses two sums over q3 configurations after reusing the message, rather than directly summing over q4 configurations. The example's message is an exact finite sum, with no simulated data. Large maximal cliques still make exact inference expensive; chordal graphs provide a decomposition, not a universal guarantee of cheap inference.[ref]

Triangulation of an undirected graph

Words: 52
Chordal graph OurBigBook.com
Triangulation adds fill edges to an undirected graph to make it a chordal graph. Given an elimination ordering, join all remaining neighbors of each removed vertex. The completed graph has that perfect elimination ordering. Fill edges can enlarge the cliques used for exact probabilistic graphical model inference, without changing the original probability factors; they do not assert new biological relationships.

Perfect elimination ordering

Words: 683 Articles: 2
Chordal graph OurBigBook.com
A perfect elimination ordering of a finite simple graph G=(V,E) is a permutation (v1​,…,vn​) of its vertices such that each set of later graph neighbours
Ni+​={vj​:j>i, {vi​,vj​}∈E}
(7)
is a clique. Thus vi​ is a simplicial vertex in the remaining induced subgraph G[{vi​,…,vn​}]. Empty and one-vertex sets satisfy the clique condition automatically. The order here is the order of deletion: v1​ goes first.
The characterization is powerful: a finite simple graph is a chordal graph if and only if it has a perfect elimination ordering. For one proof outline, the earliest vertex of an induced cycle of length at least four would have two later graph neighbours on that graph cycle that are not adjacent, contradicting the clique condition. Conversely, every nonempty chordal graph has a simplicial vertex, and every induced subgraph of a chordal graph is a chordal graph; repeatedly deleting such a vertex supplies the ordering.[ref]
In the square-plus-diagonal chordal graph above, (b,d,a,c) is a perfect elimination ordering, with later graph neighbourhoods {a,c}, {a,c}, {c}, and ∅. Starting instead with a fails: its graph neighbours b,c,d do not form a clique, because bd is absent. Thus even a chordal graph can have a poor elimination ordering.
For a larger example, join three triangles along shared edges, using
V={a,b,c,d,e},E={ab,ac,bc,bd,cd,ce,de}.
(8)
The exact graph neighbourhoods are N(a)={b,c}, N(b)={a,c,d}, N(c)={a,b,d,e}, N(d)={b,c,e}, and N(e)={c,d}. The ordering (a,b,c,d,e) has later graph neighbourhoods {b,c}, {c,d}, {d,e}, {e}, and ∅, all cliques; this certifies that the graph is a chordal graph without enumerating its graph cycles. Its maximal cliques {a,b,c}, {b,c,d}, {c,d,e} form a junction tree in that order, with intersections {b,c} and {c,d}.
To find an ordering, maximum cardinality search starts with all scores zero, repeatedly selects an unselected vertex of largest score, and increases each unselected graph neighbour's score by one. Reverse the selection order to obtain a candidate perfect elimination ordering. For the three-triangle graph, one valid selection sequence is (e,d,c,b,a), with scores at selection 0,1,2,2,2; reversing it gives the displayed deletion order. On a chordal graph every tie choice works. On an arbitrary graph, test the resulting later graph neighbourhoods for the clique condition to recognize chordal graphs. Suitable adjacency lists, score buckets and a linear-time verification method give O(∣V∣+∣E∣) recognition.[ref]
The deletion rule also explains sparse Gaussian elimination. For a symmetric positive-definite matrix whose matrix graph is G, eliminating pivot v applies the Schur complement update
auw​⟵auw​−avv​auv​avw​​.
(9)
Only pairs of remaining graph neighbours of v can acquire new off-diagonal entries. A perfect elimination ordering already has all those edges, so Cholesky decomposition creates no symbolic fill-in. Positive definiteness ensures nonzero pivots in exact arithmetic. Special numerical cancellation can suppress predicted entries, and floating-point rounding affects their values.[ref] In the three-triangle graph, deleting c first instead connects every pair in {a,b,d,e} and adds exactly ad,ae,be. The graph was already a chordal graph; the extra fill-in comes from the ordering.
One further reward is optimal graph coloring. Process a perfect elimination ordering backwards and give each vertex the smallest positive color absent from its already colored graph neighbours. Those graph neighbours form a clique, so this greedy algorithm uses at most the clique number ω(G) colors; any clique of that size requires at least that many. In the three-triangle graph, coloring (e,d,c,b,a) gives colors (1,2,3,1,2), so both the chromatic number and the clique number are three. Every maximal clique also occurs among {vi​}∪Ni+​: take its earliest vertex and use maximality. The same ordering therefore supports graph coloring, maximal clique extraction and sparse computation.
Historically, Donald J. Rose, Robert E. Tarjan and George S. Lueker's 1976 paper connected graph elimination to symmetric sparse matrices and gave a search-based O(∣V∣+∣E∣) algorithm for finding a perfect elimination ordering when one exists. Its abstract distinguishes a minimal elimination ordering from a minimum one: removing avoidable fill-in does not by itself minimize the total number of added edges.[ref]

Maximum cardinality search is a graph search in which an unselected vertex's score counts its already selected graph neighbours. Repeatedly select a vertex of maximum score, breaking ties arbitrarily, and update its unselected graph neighbours. On a chordal graph, the reverse selection order is a perfect elimination ordering. On C4​, selecting (a,b,c,d) instead yields candidate deletion order (d,c,b,a); d's later graph neighbours a,c are not adjacent, so the clique check fails.[ref]

The Johnson graph has the k-element subsets of an n-element set as vertices, with two vertices adjacent exactly when their intersection has k−1 elements. Relabelling the ground set gives graph automorphisms. The maximal cliques of a Johnson graph allow reconstruction of those ground-set labels when the two clique sizes are different.

Johnson graph OurBigBook.com
One edge of a Johnson graph replaces one element of a k-subset, so it can increase intersection with a fixed target by at most one. Replacing each element outside the target by one missing target element gives a path reaching this lower bound. Equal-distance ordered pairs have equal sizes of intersection, the two differences and the remaining ground set; a permutation matching these four regions proves distance transitivity.

Johnson graph OurBigBook.com

To see why these exhaust the possibilities, write two adjacent vertices as D∪{a} and D∪{b}. A common adjacent vertex either contains D or lies in D∪{a,b}. A vertex of the first kind outside that union is not adjacent to a vertex of the second kind omitting an element of D, so a clique cannot mix these alternatives. For J(n,3) and n≥5, n=6, the clique sizes n−2 and four distinguish the families containing pairs. Their incidence recovers J(n,2), whose stars of size n−1 distinguish the individual ground-set points from its triangular cliques.

Orientation of a graph

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A choice of direction for each edge of an undirected graph, producing a directed graph.
An orientation of a graph keeps the same vertex set and the same individual edges. For every edge {u,v} with distinct endpoints, choose exactly one directed edge, either u→v or v→u. Replacing it by both arrows is a different construction: it doubles the edges and permits travel both ways along that connection. In an orientation of a graph, the return journey must use another route.[ref]
All examples below use finite simple graphs: no self-loops and no multiple edges. For a multigraph, each individual nonloop edge receives its own direction, so two multiple edges can point in opposite directions. A self-loop becomes u→u, which is already a directed cycle of length one and therefore prevents an acyclic orientation. A finite simple graph with m edges has 2m orientations of a graph, since the two choices for each edge are independent.
Think of vertices as junctions and edges as streets. An orientation of a graph makes each street one-way; reachability asks whether a legal journey exists from one specified junction to another. Two useful aims pull in different directions: an acyclic orientation rules out circular dependencies, while a strong orientation permits journeys between every ordered pair of junctions.

Acyclic orientation

Words: 467 Articles: 2
Orientation of a graph OurBigBook.com
An acyclic orientation is an orientation of a graph whose resulting directed graph has no directed cycle, hence is a Directed acyclic graph. A directed cycle must follow every arrow around its closed route. A cycle in a graph in the skeleton of a directed graph only requires the corresponding undirected edges; their arrows need not agree around the route.
For the same triangle in a graph with vertex set {A,B,C} and edges AB,BC,AC, compare
D1​: A→B, B→C, A→C,D2​: A→B, B→C, C→A.
(10)
Both have an undirected cycle in a graph in their skeleton of a directed graph. Only D2​ has a directed cycle. In D1​, C has no outgoing directed edge, so a route cannot continue from C back to A.
Thus an acyclic orientation does not require its underlying undirected graph to be a forest. Every orientation of a graph of a forest is acyclic, because a directed cycle would give an undirected cycle in a graph. Conversely, every finite simple graph, including one with many cycles in a graph, admits at least one acyclic orientation by the following ordering construction. On this triangle in a graph, six of the eight orientations of a graph are acyclic; the other two follow the directed cycle in opposite senses.

A proper k-colouring gives an orientation from smaller to larger colours, so every directed path has strictly increasing colours and at most k vertices. Conversely, assign to each vertex the number of vertices in a longest directed path ending there. Along an edge u→v this number increases: an ending path at u cannot contain v without forming a directed cycle, so it can be extended. The resulting labels give a proper colouring using at most λ(D) colours. These two constructions prove equality. Counting edges instead of vertices in path length subtracts one from the displayed minimum.

Returning to the starting vertex would require an impossible strict increase back to the initial index, so this is an acyclic orientation. The displayed D1​ comes from A<B<C.
The chosen strict total order is a topological order of the resulting Directed acyclic graph. Conversely, every acyclic orientation of a finite simple graph has a topological order, and orienting its edges from earlier to later in that order recovers it. Different topological orders can induce the same acyclic orientation, since vertices with no edge between them need not impose a choice of arrow.[ref]
An order respects reachability but does not create it: u<v in a chosen topological order does not imply a directed path from u to v. For example, orient the two edges of the graph path A,B,C using A<C<B. The arrows are A→B and C→B; there is no directed path from A to C, despite A<C. In D1​, however, A reaches C both directly and via B. Following outgoing directed edges with graph search decides this directional reachability.[ref]

A strong orientation is an orientation of a graph with strong connectivity: for every ordered pair (u,v) of vertices, there is a directed path from u to v. A length-zero directed path permits u=v. Ordinary connectivity of the underlying undirected graph is necessary, but does not ensure this two-way reachability after directions are chosen. The acyclic D1​ is not a strong orientation; the cyclic D2​ is, since a journey can continue around its directed cycle.
Attach a new vertex D to that triangle in a graph by the single edge CD. This edge is a bridge in a graph. If oriented C→D, no directed path leaves D for the triangle in a graph; if oriented D→C, no directed path from the triangle in a graph reaches D. Neither choice gives a strong orientation, even when the triangle in a graph itself is cyclically oriented. By contrast, the four-vertex cycle graph has the strong orientation
A→B→C→D→A.
(11)
Following this directed cycle reaches any requested vertex in at most three steps. Removing any one of its undirected edges leaves a graph path through all four vertices, so it has no bridge in a graph.
For more than one vertex, a strong orientation cannot also be an acyclic orientation: directed paths from u to v and back give a nonempty closed directed walk, from which removing repeated portions leaves a directed cycle. A directed graph containing one directed cycle need not have strong connectivity, as the attached D shows.

Robbins' theorem

Words: 158
Strong orientation OurBigBook.com
A finite nonempty connected graph whose edges are undirected admits a strong orientation if and only if it has no bridge in a graph. This statement holds for finite multigraphs as well as finite simple graphs; self-loops do not help connect distinct vertices. The single-vertex case is allowed, with length-zero directed paths.[ref]
Necessity comes from the two sides separated by deleting a bridge in a graph: its chosen arrow crosses in only one direction. For sufficiency, the cited constructive proof uses depth-first search to find a cycle in a graph, orients it cyclically, contracts it, and repeats. Undoing the contractions replaces junctions by directed cycles, retaining two-way reachability. Contraction can produce multiple edges, so these must remain distinct. This is a construction outline; the input graph is finite and bridgeless, and remaining edges within contracted pieces can receive arbitrary directions.[ref]

A finite undirected graph can be oriented with outdegree at least an integer k≥0 at every vertex if and only if every vertex subset U is incident to at least k∣U∣ distinct edges. The max-flow min-cut theorem and integral max-flow theorem prove sufficiency by assigning distinct edges to vertices through an incidence flow network; each assigned edge is oriented away from that vertex. Necessity follows by counting outgoing edges from U.

A cut vertex, also called an articulation point, is a vertex v of an undirected graph whose deletion increases the number of connected components of a graph. Write k(G) for that count, including isolated vertices, and G−v for the graph obtained by removing v and every incident edge. Then the test is k(G−v)>k(G), even when the original graph is disconnected. By contrast, deleting a bridge in a graph removes just one edge and keeps both endpoint vertices. These are different failure models. [ref]
First take two triangles in a graph, ABC and ADE, sharing only the vertex A. This simple graph has
V={A,B,C,D,E},E={AB,AC,BC,AD,AE,DE}.
(12)
Here XY abbreviates the unordered pair {X,Y}. Removing A leaves the two connected components of a graph {B,C} and {D,E}, so k(G−A)=2>1=k(G). Removing any other vertex leaves a connected graph. Thus A is the only cut vertex. Every edge lies on a triangle in a graph, so deleting any single edge still leaves a graph path between its endpoints along the other two edges. There are no bridges in a graph.

V={A,B,C,D,E,F},E={AB,AC,BC,CD,DE,DF,EF}.
(13)

Deleting C also removes AC and BC, leaving connected components of a graph {A,B} and {D,E,F}. Deleting D instead leaves {A,B,C} and {E,F}. Thus C,D are exactly the cut vertices.

For a disconnected example, adjoin an isolated vertex Z to the first graph. Now k(G)=2, deleting A gives k(G−A)=3, and deleting Z gives k(G−Z)=1. The original graph was already disconnected, but A is still a cut vertex; Z is not. The empty graph has count zero, so deleting the only vertex of a one-vertex graph does not create a cut vertex. Nor is either endpoint of a single isolated edge a cut vertex, although that edge is a bridge in a graph.
In a communications network, a cut vertex models a router whose failure separates surviving routers. The shared-A example shows why having an alternative graph path around each individual edge does not protect against failure of the common router. An additional edge from B to D removes this particular vulnerability: after deleting A, B,D still join the two sides. A bridge in a graph instead models a vulnerable link. This distinction tells us whether to add another cable between existing devices or a route avoiding an indispensable device; it describes connectivity, rather than traffic capacity or failure probabilities.
The beautiful structural consequence is that a graph splits into biconnected components joined at cut vertices. Within each nontrivial robust piece, a single vertex failure cannot separate the other vertices; between pieces, the shared cut vertices reveal the bottlenecks. Also, a Hamiltonian graph has no cut vertex: deleting any vertex from its Hamilton cycle leaves a Hamiltonian path through all remaining vertices.
Historically, Tarjan's June 1972 paper developed depth-first search as a tool for finding biconnected components in time linear in the numbers of vertices and edges. [ref] In his 1983 recollection, Tarjan credited Hopcroft with the original linear-time biconnected component algorithm during their collaboration beginning in summer 1970, and described the published version as a refinement. The historical lesson is how a carefully organized traversal turns many separate deletion experiments into one computation. [ref]

Biconnected component

Words: 104

A biconnected component is a maximal connected subgraph with no cut vertex of its own. We use the block convention that also includes each bridge in a graph with its two endpoint vertices, and each isolated vertex, as a biconnected component. A biconnected component with at least three vertices stays connected after any single vertex deletion. Distinct biconnected components share at most one vertex; the vertices belonging to more than one biconnected component are exactly the cut vertices. The shared-A example has two biconnected components, its two triangles in a graph. The joined-CD example has three: ABC, the bridge in a graph CD with its endpoints, and DEF. The edges partition into these pieces, while the shared cut vertices occur in several pieces. [ref]

DFS discovery time (disc(v))

Cut vertex OurBigBook.com
The DFS discovery time of a vertex is its first-visit number in depth-first search, assigned by an increasing counter. Discovery edges form a rooted tree in each connected component of a graph. For the joined-CD example, starting at A and visiting graph neighbours in lexicographic order gives first visits A,B,C,D,E,F, numbered 1,2,3,4,5,6; its discovery edges are AB,BC,CD,DE,EF. These numbers encode the chosen traversal, not an invariant of the graph.

DFS lowpoint (low(v))

Words: 445
Cut vertex OurBigBook.com
For a finite simple graph that is an undirected graph, the DFS lowpoint of v is the smallest DFS discovery time reachable by following zero or more discovery edges down its rooted tree, then at most one non-discovery edge to an ancestor. Staying at v is allowed. Ignore the reverse traversal of the discovery edge to the parent in a rooted tree: it is the same edge, not an escape route. Start with low(v)=disc(v). On returning from a child in a rooted tree w, replace low(v) by min{low(v),low(w)}. For a non-discovery edge from v to an earlier ancestor a, replace it by min{low(v),disc(a)}. This summarizes how far upward the explored branch can reconnect. [ref]
The cut vertex criterion has a separate case for each root of a tree in the discovery forest:
  • A nonroot vertex u is a cut vertex exactly when some child in a rooted tree w satisfies low(w)≥disc(u).
  • A root of a tree is a cut vertex exactly when it has at least two children in a rooted tree, counting discovery edges, rather than all graph neighbours.
  • A discovery edge uw is a bridge in a graph exactly when low(w)>disc(u). A non-discovery edge is never a bridge in a graph.
Why does equality matter? If low(w)=disc(u), the branch below w can reconnect to u, so the discovery edge uw lies on a graph cycle and is not a bridge in a graph. Deleting the vertex u destroys that reconnection too. If u has a parent in a rooted tree, the branch is then separated from that parent in a rooted tree, explaining the non-strict cut vertex test. For a root of a tree, there is no earlier side to separate from; distinct discovery branches cannot have an edge between them, since depth-first search would have explored them as one branch. This gives the two-children in a rooted tree rule. These are proof outlines of the criteria. [ref][ref]
In the joined-CD example with DFS discovery times 1,2,3,4,5,6, the DFS lowpoints in label order are 1,1,1,4,4,4. For C and its child in a rooted tree D, 4>3: CD is a bridge in a graph, and C is a cut vertex. For D and its child in a rooted tree E, 4=4: D is a cut vertex, although DE is not a bridge in a graph. The root of a tree A has only one child in a rooted tree, B, so it is not a cut vertex. In the shared-A example, the root of a tree A has two children in a rooted tree, B and D, and is a cut vertex, while every DFS lowpoint is 1 and no edge passes the strict bridge in a graph test.
Restart depth-first search at every undiscovered vertex to cover a disconnected graph, applying the root of a tree rule separately in each connected component of a graph. With adjacency lists and constant-cost label operations, computing all DFS lowpoints, cut vertices and bridges in a graph has time complexity O(∣V∣+∣E∣) in Big O notation, because each vertex is discovered once and each edge is inspected twice. The simple parent-skipping rule assumes a simple graph. In a multigraph, skip only the actual parent edge, identified individually: a parallel edge to the same parent in a rooted tree is a valid reconnection and can prevent the first edge from being a bridge in a graph. The criteria here concern undirected graphs; a directed graph requires a different connectivity analysis.

Walk in a graph (v0​,e1​,v1​,…,em​,vm​)

Words: 1k Articles: 2
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A walk records a journey through a graph as a finite alternating sequence
W=(v0​,e1​,v1​,…,em​,vm​),m≥0,
(14)
where each edge ei​ joins the consecutive vertices vi−1​ and vi​. Both vertices and edges may repeat. Its length is m, counting edge traversals with repetitions, rather than counting different edges or measuring the drawing. Here a graph path means a walk with no repeated vertices; a trail instead forbids repeated edges. These conventions distinguish a journey's record from the subgraph consisting of the connections it used.[ref]
Unless stated otherwise, the examples below use a finite simple graph that is an undirected graph, so an edge may be traversed in either direction. In a multigraph, retain each edge's individual identity as well as its endpoint vertices: two parallel edges are different choices for the same step. If self-loops are allowed, traversing one leaves the current vertex unchanged but adds one to the length. In a directed graph, each step must follow its directed edge from its initial to its terminal vertex, giving a directed walk; reversing a journey need not be possible.[ref]
We allow the zero-length walk (v) at every vertex v. It uses no edges, so it is also a trail and a graph path, and its coinciding endpoints make it a closed walk. This means staying put is a legitimate journey; a graph with no vertices has no such walk. Positive-length restrictions will be stated explicitly.[ref]
Use the same constructed graph throughout these three sections:
V={A,B,C,D,E,F},E={AB,BC,CA,AD,DE,EA,AF}.
(15)
Here AB denotes the unordered pair {A,B}, and CA=AC. Two triangles in a graph, ABC and ADE, share A, with one extra edge AF. These are schematic connections, not measured roads; the highlighted connections in the diagram show which edges are used, while the numbered sequence records their order.
The length-six walk B,C,A,B,C,A,F uses BC and CA twice, so it is not a trail. The length-six trail B,C,A,D,E,A,F returns to A but uses six different edges, so it is not a graph path. The length-three graph path B,C,A,F repeats neither vertices nor edges. Thus
{graph paths}⊊{trails}⊊{walks}
(16)
for this particular graph. The restrictions answer different routing questions: revisiting a junction is harmless for many journeys, whereas reusing a serviced road segment can matter for an inspection route. Travel costs require a weighted graph; a walk's cost adds the weight of each traversal, even when an edge is used again.
Every finite walk from s to t contains a graph path from s to t after deleting detours. For a proof outline, if vi​=vj​ with i<j, delete the intervening closed walk. The retained steps still meet at the same vertex, and the length strictly decreases. Repeating terminates with no repeated vertices, or with the zero-length graph path when s=t. This explains why reachability can be formulated using either walks or graph paths. With nonnegative edge weights, deletion also cannot increase cost, connecting the argument to the shortest path problem; with negative weights that cost conclusion fails.[ref]

Trail in a graph

Words: 269
Walk in a graph OurBigBook.com
A trail is a walk whose edge sequence e1​,…,em​ has no repetitions. Its vertices may repeat, including its first and last vertices. The zero-length walk is a trail because it repeats no edge. Every graph path is a trail, but the converse fails: the trail in the shared example is
B,BC,C,CA,A,AD,D,DE,E,EA,A,AF,F.
(17)
Its six edges BC,CA,AD,DE,EA,AF are pairwise distinct, although A occurs twice. Visiting a junction again and traversing a road segment again are different events.[ref]
In an undirected graph, traversing AB and then BA repeats the same edge; direction of travel does not give it a new identity. In a multigraph with distinct parallel edges p,q joining X and Y, the closed walk (X,p,Y,q,X) is a trail, whereas (X,p,Y,p,X) is not. Both have the same vertex sequence X,Y,X. In a directed graph, separate directed edges X→Y and Y→X may instead be used once each; record their identities and obey their directions. Thus testing a trail means checking the actual edge records, not merely checking consecutive endpoint labels.
For a finite graph, a trail has length at most ∣E∣; unrestricted walks can have arbitrarily large length whenever a positive-length closed walk exists, since it can be repeated. An Eulerian trail is the special trail that uses every edge, so its length is exactly ∣E∣. Our length-six trail omits AB and is therefore not an Eulerian trail. In a road-inspection model, a trail describes servicing its selected segments once while allowing returns to junctions; requiring service of every segment leads to the Eulerian trail question. If extra travel between serviced segments is necessary, the complete journey can be a walk even when each segment is serviced only once. This distinction keeps the service requirement separate from the route actually travelled.

Closed walk (vm​=v0​)

Words: 519
Walk in a graph OurBigBook.com
A closed walk is a walk with equal endpoint vertices, vm​=v0​. Under our convention this includes the zero-length walk (v); returning after traversing at least one edge requires m>0. Closure imposes no other restriction on repeated vertices or edges. In a directed graph, a closed directed walk must also follow every directed edge in its permitted direction.[ref]
In the shared simple graph, A,F,A is a length-two closed walk that immediately backtracks along AF. It is not a trail, since AF is used twice, and it is not a graph cycle. The length-six closed walk A,B,C,A,D,E,A is a trail, since its six edges are distinct, but is not a graph cycle: it returns to A midway through the journey. The length-three closed walk A,B,C,A is a graph cycle, with all vertices distinct apart from the required endpoint repetition. In a simple graph that is an undirected graph, a graph cycle has length at least three; the two-step backtrack is excluded.[ref]
A positive-length closed walk therefore need not reveal a graph cycle: even a tree permits an out-and-back journey on an edge. A positive-length closed trail in a simple graph does contain a graph cycle. For a proof outline, choose a shortest positive-length consecutive portion of the trail whose endpoint vertices coincide. It cannot repeat an internal vertex, since that would give a shorter such portion; it cannot have length one or two because self-loops and repeated edges are excluded. It is consequently a graph cycle. Cutting it out leaves another closed trail, possibly of length zero, so repetition partitions the original edges into graph cycles. In our six-step example these are the two triangles in a graph. A closed trail using every edge would be an Euler circuit; here AF is omitted.
Counting return journeys makes closed walks useful even when they repeat edges. For a finite simple graph with adjacency matrix M, the walk count from powers of an adjacency matrix gives (Mk)uv​ length-k walks from u to v, for every nonnegative integer k. A proof outline is that matrix multiplication appends one allowed step, summing over the previous endpoint; M0 is the identity matrix, recording the unique zero-length walk at each vertex. Consequently
(Mk)vv​=#{length-k closed walks starting at v},tr(Mk)=∑v∈V​(Mk)vv​.
(18)
The trace counts closed walks with a specified starting vertex and traversal order, not distinct graph cycles. These formulas use adjacency entries, not arbitrary travel costs in a weighted graph.[ref]
In our example, (M2)AA​=5: the five length-two closed walks are A,B,A, A,C,A, A,D,A, A,E,A, and A,F,A. Also (M3)AA​=4, going round either triangle in a graph in either direction, and tr(M3)=12: each of the two triangles in a graph supplies three choices of starting vertex and two directions. These exact counts for the constructed graph illustrate why return counts and graph cycle counts differ.
A closed walk naturally models a delivery or inspection journey that returns to its depot. Repeated vertices let it combine several excursions; repeated edges let it serve a dead end and return. For an Euclidean travelling salesman tour, one can first construct a closed walk visiting all locations and then use the triangle inequality to shortcut repeated visits without increasing total length. That argument assumes direct travel between the retained locations is permitted, as in a complete graph weighted by Euclidean distance; an arbitrary road network need not contain those shortcut edges.

Vertex cover

Words: 990 Articles: 8
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A vertex cover chooses vertices that collectively touch every edge of a graph. Think of placing monitors at junctions: if a monitor watches every connection incident to its junction, a vertex cover watches all connections. The minimum vertex cover asks how few monitors suffice. This is a model of covering connections through their endpoints, rather than of monitoring distances in the drawing.
For a finite simple graph G=(V,E), a vertex cover is a subset C⊆V satisfying
{u,v}∈E⟹u∈C or v∈C.
(19)
Both endpoints may be selected; the condition requires at least one. An isolated vertex covers no edge, so a minimum vertex cover never needs it.[ref]
Take the cycle graph C5​ with vertices 0,1,2,3,4 and edges 01,12,23,34,40. The set C={1,3,4} is a vertex cover: vertex 1 covers 01 and 12, vertex 3 covers 23 and 34, and vertex 4 covers 40 as well as 34. In particular, the closing edge 40 is covered even though vertex 0 is unselected.
The unselected vertices I=V∖C={0,2} form an independent set. This is the key connection: an edge missed by C would have both endpoints in I, precisely what an independent set forbids. For every subset C⊆V,
C is a vertex cover⟺V∖C is an independent set.
(20)
Here V∖C is the complement of a set within V; the graph itself keeps all its edges. The complement graph is a different construction.[ref]
The endpoints of any maximal matching form a vertex cover: an edge avoiding all endpoints would enlarge that matching in a graph. Consequently a graph with no matching in a graph of size s has a vertex cover of size at most 2(s−1). This supplies a convenient vertex cover, but it need not be a minimum vertex cover.

Isolated vertices can be ignored when exactly one component contains all the edges. The edge-free case depends on whether the empty solution is admitted.

Vertex cover decision problem ((G,k): τ(G)≤k)

Words: 67
Vertex cover OurBigBook.com
The vertex cover decision problem asks whether a finite simple graph G has a vertex cover containing at most k vertices. For an uncovered edge uv, any valid vertex cover contains u or v. Branch on these two possibilities, delete the chosen vertex and its incident edges, and decrease k by one. An edgeless graph accepts and a nonempty graph with k=0 rejects. The search tree has at most 2k leaves, giving running time O(2k(∣V∣+∣E∣)) with straightforward copying. Thus this parameterization is fixed-parameter tractable.

Independent vertex cover

Vertex cover OurBigBook.com
An independent vertex cover is a vertex cover that is also an independent set. Its complement is an independent set as well, since the cover condition forbids edges entirely in that complement. Thus such a cover is a side of a bipartition of the graph. This standard definition is stronger than independent dominating set on graphs without isolated vertices, and remains a different notion when isolated vertices are present. In a nonempty simple graph, two possibly repeated witnesses x,y with ¬E(x,y) and no edge outside {x,y} express existence of an independent vertex cover of size at most two.

Minimum vertex cover

Vertex cover OurBigBook.com
A minimum vertex cover is a vertex cover of smallest cardinality among all vertex covers of the same finite simple graph. The optimum size is the vertex cover number. By the complement of a set correspondence, a minimum vertex cover leaves a largest possible independent set unselected.
Minimum size is stronger than merely being unable to remove a selected vertex. In the star graph K1,3​, the three leaves form a vertex cover from which no vertex can be removed: each leaf covers its own edge. Nevertheless, the centre alone is a minimum vertex cover of size one. Such an inclusion-minimal vertex cover can therefore be much larger than a minimum vertex cover.

Root a finite tree, and let D0​,D1​ be the optimum vertex cover sizes of a descendant subtree conditional on excluding or including its root. Excluding a parent forces all children to be included; including it permits either child state. These facts prove the displayed recurrences by structural induction. Empty child sums give D0​=0,D1​=1 at a leaf of a rooted tree. Evaluating in postorder traversal and taking the smaller root state gives a linear-time dynamic programming algorithm.

The vertex cover number records the size of a minimum vertex cover:
τ(G)=min{∣C∣:C⊆V(G), C is a vertex cover of G}.
(21)
The vertex cover number is a number, while a minimum vertex cover is a set attaining it. For the cycle graph C5​, the independence number is 2, so the complement correspondence gives τ(C5​)=5−2=3. The vertex cover {1,3,4} above attains this size.
Every matching in a graph gives a lower bound on the vertex cover number. Its edges have no shared endpoints, so covering each selected edge requires a different vertex. Thus, for any matching in a graph M and any vertex cover C,
∣M∣≤∣C∣,ν(G)≤τ(G),
(22)
where ν(G) is the matching number. Exhibiting a matching in a graph and a vertex cover of the same size certifies that both are optimum. Kőnig's theorem for bipartite matching says that every finite bipartite graph admits this equality: ν(G)=τ(G).[ref]
For the complete bipartite graph K2,3​, let the left vertices be L={a,b} and the right vertices be R={x,y,z}. All six edges join L to R. Selecting C=L covers every edge; selecting M={ax,by} gives a matching in a graph of size two. The lower bound and this vertex cover give 2≤τ(K2,3​)≤2, so τ(K2,3​)=ν(K2,3​)=2. The remaining vertices R form a largest independent set of size three. Crossings of drawn edges are not extra vertices.
The bipartite graph hypothesis matters. In a triangle in a graph, any two vertices form a minimum vertex cover, while any two edges share an endpoint. Hence τ(K3​)=2 and ν(K3​)=1. Similarly, the cycle graph C5​ has τ(C5​)=3 and ν(C5​)=2. The inequality for the matching number remains valid, but equality can fail.

Independent set (graph theory)

Graph theory OurBigBook.com
An independent set selects mutually compatible objects when an edge of a graph represents a conflict. For example, if vertices are activities and edges join activities that cannot occur together, an independent set is a collection that can share one time slot. Finding the largest such collection is measured by the independence number.[ref]
In a finite simple graph G=(V,E), an independent set is a subset I⊆V with no edge joining two selected vertices:
u,v∈I, u=v⟹{u,v}∈/E.
(29)
The empty set and every singleton set are independent sets. In the cycle graph C5​ drawn under vertex cover, {0,2} is an independent set, but {0,4} is not: the closing edge 40 joins those two vertices. Choosing nonconsecutive labels is insufficient unless the wraparound edge is checked.
An independent set of maximum size has cardinality equal to the independence number. Being unable to add another vertex only makes an independent set inclusion-maximal. In the star graph K1,3​, the centre alone is inclusion-maximal, since it is adjacent to every leaf, but the three leaves form a larger independent set. This distinction mirrors the difference between an inclusion-minimal vertex cover and a minimum vertex cover.
Every independent set I has a vertex cover V∖I as its complement of a set; a largest independent set has a minimum vertex cover as its complement. In every proper vertex colouring, each colour class is an independent set, so graph coloring partitions the vertices into mutually compatible groups.

Maximum independent set OurBigBook.com
Root a finite tree. The two dynamic programming states are the optimal size in the descendant subtree when its root v is included, I(v), or excluded, O(v). The sums run over its children. Inclusion forces every child to be excluded; exclusion permits each child's better state. Child subtrees have no edges between them, which proves independence of these choices. The leaf states are I=1,O=0, and the root's better state gives the optimum.
A postorder traversal computes the states in O(n) time and storage. Reconstruct a set by following an attaining root choice and the same child constraints, breaking ties arbitrarily. The empty and singleton cases use the ordinary non-strict subset convention.

An independent dominating set is simultaneously an independent set and a dominating set. Equivalently, it is an independent set maximal under inclusion: an outside vertex can be added while preserving independence exactly when it has no neighbour in the selected set. On a triangle in a graph, any singleton is an independent dominating set but no independent vertex cover exists. Independence and domination are directly expressible in first-order logic when a fixed bound on the number of selected vertices is given.

For a graph whose vertices are partitioned into parts, an independent transversal is an independent set containing exactly one vertex from each part. If a cycle's parts each have twelve vertices, choose one vertex uniformly and independently per part. A cycle edge joining distinct parts is selected at both ends with probability 1/144. The independence number is the largest cardinality of an independent set in a finite simple graph:
α(G)=max{∣I∣:I⊆V(G), I is an independent set of G}.
(30)
It answers "how many mutually compatible objects can be selected at once?", while the chromatic number asks how many compatible groups are needed for all the vertices. Diestel uses this notation for a largest independent set.[ref]
For the cycle graph C5​, the independent set {0,2} shows that α(C5​)≥2. Three selected vertices would require at least three unselected vertices separating them around the cycle graph, which has only five vertices. Thus α(C5​)=2. There are five largest independent sets, obtained by rotating {0,2} around the cycle graph, and five corresponding minimum vertex covers.
For the complete bipartite graph K2,3​, an independent set cannot contain a vertex from each side, since every such pair is joined by an edge. The larger side has three vertices, so α(K2,3​)=3. A triangle in a graph has independence number one. A graph with no edges and n vertices has independence number n, including α(G)=0 when n=0.

τ(G)+α(G)=n.

Every extra vertex that can be left in an independent set is one fewer vertex needed in a minimum vertex cover. This identity holds for all finite simple graphs, including the triangle in a graph and the cycle graph C5​; it does not require the bipartite graph hypothesis of Kőnig's theorem for bipartite matching.

Words: 1k Articles: 5

A Hamilton cycle, also called a Hamiltonian cycle, is a cycle in a graph containing every vertex of the graph. Here the convention is a finite simple graph whose edges are undirected, with n=∣V∣≥3. A traversal is a sequence
v0​,v1​,…,vn−1​,vn​=v0​,
(36)
where v0​,…,vn−1​ are all the distinct vertices and {vi​,vi+1​}∈E for 0≤i<n. Thus "once" means once before the closing return: the start appears again at the end, and there are exactly n traversed edges. The graph may contain additional unused edges.[ref]
A Hamiltonian path visits all vertices once without requiring a return. Removing an edge from a Hamilton cycle gives a Hamiltonian path; a particular Hamiltonian path closes only if its endpoints are adjacent. An Euler circuit instead traverses every edge exactly once and can revisit vertices midway. The two requirements are independent, as these original labelled examples show.
For the complete graph K4​, use V={A,B,C,D} and E={AB,AC,AD,BC,BD,CD}, where AB abbreviates the unordered pair {A,B}. The route A,B,C,D,A is a Hamilton cycle: it visits every vertex and uses four of the six edges, omitting AC and BD. It is not an Euler circuit, and the graph admits no Euler circuit at all: every vertex degree is three, contradicting the Euler circuit criterion. The crossing of the drawn diagonals is not another vertex.
Conversely, take two triangles in a graph sharing only X, with V={X,A,B,C,D} and E={XA,AB,BX,XC,CD,DX}. The route X,A,B,X,C,D,X is an Euler circuit, using all six edges once; the vertex degrees are 4,2,2,2,2. It cannot be a Hamilton cycle, since X occurs midway as well as at the start and end. More strongly, no Hamilton cycle exists: X is a cut vertex, and deleting it leaves the two separate edges AB and CD. Nevertheless, A,B,X,C,D is a Hamiltonian path, whose endpoints are not adjacent.

Ore's theorem, named after Øystein Ore, says that a finite simple graph with n≥3 vertices is Hamiltonian if every nonadjacent pair has degree sum at least n.
For a proof, enlarge a hypothetical counterexample to an edge-maximal non-Hamiltonian graph. Adding a missing edge uv creates a Hamiltonian cycle, hence the original graph has a Hamiltonian path u=v1​,…,vn​=v. If both uvi+1​ and vvi​ are edges, the path closes to a cycle by reversing its final segment. Thus the index sets of these two kinds of edges are disjoint in {1,…,n−1}, giving d(u)+d(v)≤n−1, a contradiction. The degree condition is sufficient and need not follow from a lower bound of n/2 on every individual degree.
Necessary conditions for a Hamilton cycle
Words: 142
Hamilton cycle OurBigBook.com
A Hamiltonian graph must be a connected graph and have minimum degree δ(G)≥2: each vertex has two distinct neighbours on its Hamilton cycle. It also has no cut vertex. Indeed, deleting any vertex from the Hamilton cycle leaves a graph path through every remaining vertex, so the remaining graph is connected. These are quick ways to rule out a Hamilton cycle.[ref]
Even these conditions together are not sufficient: the complete bipartite graph K2,3​ is connected, has minimum degree two and no cut vertex, but has no Hamilton cycle. Every graph cycle in a bipartite graph alternates between its two parts, using equally many vertices from each; it cannot use all two and all three.
In the other direction, Dirac's theorem gives a sufficient condition: a finite simple graph with n≥3 and δ(G)≥n/2 has a Hamilton cycle. Failure of this inequality proves nothing by itself: the cycle graph C5​ has a Hamilton cycle despite δ(C5​)=2<5/2.[ref]
Weighted Hamilton cycle (L(C)=∑e∈E(C)​we​)
Words: 344
Hamilton cycle OurBigBook.com
A weighted Hamilton cycle is a Hamilton cycle in a weighted graph, with cost equal to the sum of its traversed edge weights. Here weights represent symmetric nonnegative costs, rather than conductances. Asking whether a Hamilton cycle exists is a feasibility question; asking for the cheapest one is an instance of the travelling salesman problem. A complete graph supplies every possible connection between distinct vertices, making feasibility automatic for n≥3, while choosing the cheapest visiting order remains a separate mathematical optimization problem.
Assign the complete graph K4​ the symmetric edge costs wAB​=2, wBC​=3, wCD​=4, wAD​=5, wAC​=6 and wBD​=7, in arbitrary units. Fix the start at A and identify each Hamilton cycle with its reverse. The three possibilities are
A,B,C,D,AA,B,D,C,AA,C,B,D,A​:2+3+4+5=14,:2+7+4+6=19,:6+3+7+5=21.​
(37)
These exhaust the possibilities: the permutations of the other three vertices give 3!=6 orders, paired into three reversals. Hence the perimeter tour really is optimal for this toy instance. The diagram's geometric lengths are not costs, and no triangle inequality is assumed.
The usefulness of this model is to distinguish visiting required sites from covering required connections. If tasks are assigned to vertices and the route must return after one visit to each, a weighted Hamilton cycle captures the ordering requirement. If the job instead requires each edge once, the relevant object is an Euler circuit. The shortest path problem asks only for a cheapest route between specified endpoints. A 1954 primary research paper gave a concrete motivation for the travelling salesman problem: certify that a particular tour through 49 cities has minimum road-distance cost.[ref]
These are abstract route models. If a cost stands for a whole graph path through an underlying network, travelling between consecutive task vertices can pass through intermediate network vertices more than once. One visit per task therefore does not imply one visit per physical junction. One-way connections require a directed graph; changing costs or extra timing constraints require a richer model than the fixed symmetric toy instance.

Complete graph (Kn​)

Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A complete graph is a simple graph in which every two distinct vertices are joined by an edge. The finite complete graph on n vertices is denoted Kn​. Here the edges are undirected, and self-loops are excluded. The usual pictures below use n≥1: K1​ is a single vertex, K2​ a single edge, and K3​ a triangle in a graph.[ref]
Completeness describes all the possible pairs, rather than a drawing style. Different layouts can represent the same graph through a graph isomorphism. Crossing lines away from the drawn vertices do not add new vertices or edges.
There are (2n​)=n(n−1)/2 unordered pairs of distinct vertices, so this is the edge count of a complete graph. Each vertex has vertex degree n−1. The degree-sum formula gives the same count: 2∣E∣=n(n−1). These formulas make a complete graph the upper extreme for edge counts among simple graphs of a fixed size.
This is useful when modelling pairwise relationships. If every pair of objects needs its own direct connection, ten vertices require 45 edges, while twenty require 190. Adding one more vertex to Kn​ introduces n further edges. This counts a specified direct-link model; it does not require every communication system to implement every relationship with a separate physical connection.
A proper vertex coloring of Kn​ must give every vertex a different color, so its chromatic number is n. For n≥1, its independence number is 1: two distinct vertices already have an edge between them. Thus complete graphs provide immediate test cases for graph coloring and independent sets.

A clique in a simple graph G is a set C of vertices such that every pair of distinct members is adjacent. Equivalently, its induced subgraph G[C] is a complete graph. The surrounding graph need not itself be complete: a clique describes complete pairwise connectivity within a selected group.
Consider the original graph with
V={a,b,c,d,e},E={ab,ac,bc,cd,de}.
(39)
The set {a,b,c} is a clique because all three pairs ab,ac,bc are edges. The set {b,c,d} is not a clique: the edge bd is missing. A path in a graph connecting all selected vertices is therefore insufficient; every pair must have a direct edge.
Here the clique number is 3. The maximum clique is {a,b,c}, but {c,d} and {d,e} are also maximal cliques. This distinction is useful when an algorithm stops as soon as its current clique cannot be enlarged: that stopping condition establishes maximality, while finding the largest possible clique is a separate requirement.

A maximal clique is a clique not strictly contained in another clique. This is distinct from a maximum clique, whose size equals the clique number. In a triangulated probabilistic graphical model, maximal cliques are the natural nodes of a junction tree.
Maximality is a condition on set inclusion: no outside vertex is adjacent to every member of the current clique. In the five-vertex example, {c,d} is maximal because a,b are not adjacent to d, while e is not adjacent to c. Yet {a,b,c} is larger. Checking every possible one-vertex extension is enough: if a larger containing clique existed, any one of its new vertices could already be added.[ref]

Eulerian graph

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
An Eulerian graph has an Euler circuit: a closed trail traversing every edge exactly once. Here the graph is a finite undirected graph, possibly a multigraph with self-loops. Parallel edges retain distinct identities, and each self-loop contributes two to its vertex degree. Repeated vertices are allowed. This models inspecting every road segment once, even when a junction must be revisited.
For a nonempty set of edges, the Euler circuit criterion requires a connected graph only on the edge support of a graph: isolated vertices impose no travel requirement. A single vertex with a self-loop and two vertices joined by two parallel edges are both Eulerian graphs. Neither requires three vertices. With no edges and at least one vertex, we allow the zero-length trail at that vertex as an Euler circuit; the graph with no vertices has no such walk.
The motivating Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem asks for an Eulerian trail, which need not return to its starting vertex. In Leonhard Euler's Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis by Leonhard Euler, §2 poses the bridge-crossing question and §§4–6 encode land regions by letters. The river's shape drops out: only the connections matter. The paper was written in 1735 and published in 1741, according to the Euler Archive; the journal volume carries the nominal year 1736.[ref]

For a finite undirected multigraph G=(V,E), its edge support of a graph is the subgraph G+​=(V+​,E) with V+​={v∈V:deg(v)>0}. It removes exactly the isolated vertices, retaining every edge, including self-loops and parallel edges. When E=∅, connectivity of this subgraph is the relevant condition for an Eulerian trail or Euler circuit.
