Model the four land regions by vertices A,B,C,D and the seven bridges by distinct edges: two AB, two AC, and one each of AD,BD,CD. Their vertex degrees are (5,3,3,3). Leonhard Euler's paper records these connections in §6 and the obstruction in §9; §20 states the zero-or-two odd-region rule. Four odd vertex degrees exclude an Eulerian trail, even if returning to the starting vertex is optional.[ref]

Eulerian trail

Words: 279 Articles: 1
Eulerian graph OurBigBook.com
An Eulerian trail, also called an Eulerian path, is a trail in a graph traversing every edge exactly once. The name Eulerian path does not require a graph path: vertices may repeat. A Hamiltonian path instead visits every vertex exactly once, and may omit edges. An Eulerian trail may omit isolated vertices, so these are different coverage requirements.
For a finite undirected multigraph with at least one edge, allowing self-loops, an Eulerian trail exists exactly when the edge support of a graph is a connected graph and there are zero or two vertices of odd vertex degree. In the two-odd-vertex case they must be the two distinct endpoints; in the zero-odd-vertex case every Eulerian trail is an Euler circuit. Count a self-loop twice in the vertex degree but once in the trail, and count each parallel edge separately.[ref]
The parity obstruction is local: each intermediate visit pairs an arriving edge with a departing edge. Only the distinct endpoints can have an unpaired incidence. The handshaking lemma, ∑v∈V​deg(v)=2∣E∣, also shows that the number of vertices with odd vertex degree is even. Sufficiency in the two-endpoint case reduces to the Euler circuit criterion: add one extra edge between the odd vertices, construct an Euler circuit, rotate its record to start with the extra edge, then delete that edge. The remaining trail has the required endpoints.
For the Seven Bridges of Königsberg multigraph, the vertex degrees at A,B,C,D are (5,3,3,3), so no Eulerian trail exists. Remove the unique edge AD: the vertex degrees become (4,3,3,2), and a six-edge Eulerian trail runs from B to C. Label the parallel edges p1​,p2​ between A,B and q1​,q2​ between A,C; label BD by r and CD by s. A complete record is B,p1​,A,q1​,C,s,D,r,B,p2​,A,q2​,C. It revisits A,B,C while using every remaining edge once.

Euler circuit

Words: 157
Eulerian graph OurBigBook.com
An Euler circuit, also called an Euler tour, is an Eulerian trail whose final vertex equals its initial vertex. Its length is ∣E∣. It can revisit other vertices, unlike a Hamiltonian cycle, which visits each vertex once before returning to the start. For a finite undirected multigraph with at least one edge, an Euler circuit exists exactly when the edge support of a graph is a connected graph and every vertex degree is even.
For example, let p,q be distinct parallel edges joining A,B, let ℓ be a self-loop at A, and add an isolated vertex Z. Then (deg(A),deg(B),deg(Z))=(4,2,0), and A,ℓ,A,p,B,q,A is an Euler tour. The self-loop supplies one traversal and two incidences; Z need not be visited. Replacing p,q by a single edge changes both vertex degrees to odd numbers and removes the possibility of an Euler circuit. Thus collapsing parallel edges can change the answer.
Two triangles in a graph sharing one vertex A give another instructive Euler circuit: A,B,C,A,D,E,A. The shared vertex has vertex degree four, the others have vertex degree two, and A is revisited between the two closed trails. This is precisely the splice used by Hierholzer's algorithm.

Euler circuit criterion

Words: 376 Articles: 1
Eulerian graph OurBigBook.com
Let G=(V,E) be a finite undirected multigraph, allowing self-loops and distinct parallel edges, with E=∅. Then
G has an Euler circuit⟺G+​ is connected and deg(v)≡0(mod2) for every v∈V,
(56)
where G+​ is the edge support of a graph, and vertex degrees count each self-loop twice. There is no lower bound of three on the number of vertices. If E=∅, the zero-length convention gives an Euler circuit exactly when V=∅.[ref]
The two requirements are independent: two separate vertices, each carrying a self-loop, have even vertex degrees but disconnected edge support of a graph, so no Euler circuit can cover both edges.
Necessity follows because a single trail cannot cover edges in different connected components of a graph, while a closed trail pairs all arriving and departing incidences, including those at its starting vertex. For sufficiency, extend a trail using unused edges until no extension is possible. Even vertex degree parity prevents it from stopping anywhere except its starting vertex: a different stopping vertex would have an odd number of used incidences and hence at least one unused incidence. The result is a closed trail.
If unused edges remain, connectivity of the edge support of a graph supplies a vertex on the current closed trail with an unused incident edge. Removing a closed trail leaves even unused vertex degrees, so the same argument constructs another closed trail from that vertex. Splice it into the existing record. The two trails use disjoint edge identities, so the splice repeats no edge. Each splice uses more edges; finiteness ensures termination with an Euler circuit. This is the constructive idea of Hierholzer's algorithm.
In the drawing, arrows indicate the chosen traversal direction along undirected edges. The first closed trail uses AB,BC,CA and the second uses AD,DE,EA. Insert the second at the final occurrence of A in A,B,C,A, giving A,B,C,A,D,E,A. A reader can check consecutive endpoints, closure, and the six distinct edges directly. With multigraphs, perform the same check on edge identities, since endpoint pairs alone cannot distinguish parallel edges.

Words: 58

Hierholzer's algorithm constructs an Euler circuit by growing closed trails along unused edges and splicing them at shared vertices, as in the Euler circuit criterion. Each edge must have a distinct record. An implementation using adjacency lists, a stack, and a used flag for each edge runs in O(∣V∣+∣E∣) time, including the connectivity and vertex degree checks. Store both incidences of a self-loop, while marking its single edge record used only once.

Tournament (graph theory) OurBigBook.com
A median order maximizes the number of forward directed edges in a linear ordering of the vertices of a tournament. Every interval inherits a median order. Moving the first vertex of an interval to its end proves that it has at least as many outgoing as incoming edges in that interval; otherwise the move would increase the number of forward edges. Reversing all edges and the order gives the dual assertion for the last vertex.

Median order of a tournament OurBigBook.com
A graph embedding into an ordered tournament is half-sparse when the displayed inequality holds for every proper final interval I. Reserving two extra tournament vertices allows extension at any outward-oriented leaf: the median order of a tournament supplies at least half of the later vertices as outneighbours of the parent's image, while half-sparsity leaves at least one of them unused. Adding one image while extending every old final interval by two preserves the inequality.

A directed cycle in an edge-weighted graph whose total weight is negative. Repeating it makes walk costs arbitrarily small. A spanning circuit family is a collection of directed cycles whose union contains every vertex of the directed graph. Different circuits may overlap. This is distinct from a cycle cover of a directed graph, which requires vertex-disjoint cycles.
Circuit-cover bound by independence number (#circuits≤α(D))
Words: 105
Spanning circuit family OurBigBook.com
For a nontrivial strongly connected directed graph, a coherent cyclic order of a digraph and the Dilworth theorem produce a spanning circuit family with at most its independence number circuits. Put a largest consecutive stable block first and duplicate its vertices as sinks. Use forward edges and edges into the sink copies to form an acyclic auxiliary graph. Its reachability order has width equal to the block size. Expand a chain partition to paths, then exchange intersecting path suffixes until the permutation of source-to-sink labels has as many cycles as possible. Paths in the same permutation cycle are disjoint, so identifying copied endpoints produces simple directed circuits. A windmill of directed triangles sharing one vertex shows that the bound is sharp.

A relation on states of labelled transition systems matching every transition with a transition of the same label in either direction, with successor states again related. The Spoiler takes one successor step from the current vertex of either rooted directed graph; the Duplicator must take a matching successor step in the other. A winning strategy gives a bisimulation by collecting endpoint pairs of all finite plays consistent with it.

For adjacent vertices u,v, the bipartite graph between N(u)∖{v} and N(v)∖{u} has degree two at every vertex, forcing d(u)=d(v). Thus the graph is regular. Counting second neighbours gives 3(n−d−1)=d(d−1). The nontrivial adjacency eigenvalues are (−3±4d−3​)/2, and the larger-root multiplicity is [n−1+d2/4d−3​]/2. Integrality forces t=4d−3​ to be an odd integer dividing 9, yielding the stated degrees. The complete bipartite graph K3,3​ realizes degree three. The one-vertex graph is a vacuous exception with degree zero.

Four-connected planar obstruction to two-linkage

Words: 87
Linked graph OurBigBook.com
On vertices 0,…,7, join cyclic indices differing by one or two modulo eight. The resulting planar graph has a square face bounded in order by 0,2,4,6. Deleting at most three vertices cannot disconnect it: each break in the surviving cyclic chain requires two consecutive deleted vertices, and two separate breaks require four deletions. It is therefore four-connected. Disjoint paths joining 0 to 4 and 2 to 6 would cross in the complementary disk of the square face, contrary to the Jordan curve theorem. Thus four-connectivity does not guarantee two-linkage.

Rooted dense minor linkage (2δ(H)≥∣H∣+4k−1)

Words: 97
Linked graph OurBigBook.com
If a graph is 2k-connected and has a graph minor H satisfying 2δ(H)≥∣H∣+4k−1, it is k-linked. Write d=∣H∣−1−δ(H), so ∣H∣≥2d+4k+1. The rooted branch-set reduction replaces the minor model by ∣H∣−k disjoint connected sets, the first 2k containing any prescribed terminals separately, each missing at most d of the remaining sets. Every prescribed pair then has at least k+1 common adjacent unused sets, allowing the k connections to be selected successively. The reduction uses rooted separations of a graph, contraction of edges outside distinct branch sets, and a final Hall marriage theorem matching; the separation condition prevents a contraction from destroying access to the model.

Graph subdivision (TH)

Words: 301 Articles: 3
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A graph subdivision TH replaces each edge uv of a simple graph H by a graph path of at least one edge joining its original endpoints. The original vertices are branch vertices of a graph subdivision. The replacement graph paths have pairwise disjoint interiors, contain no branch vertices of a graph subdivision internally, and together make up the entire new graph. Leaving an edge unchanged is allowed.[ref]
For an explicit example, take H with vertex set {A,B,C,D} and edges AB,BC,CA,AD: a triangle in a graph with one attached leaf of a graph. Replace its edges by the following branch paths of a graph subdivision:
PAB​=(A,x,B),PBC​=(B,y,z,C),PCA​=(C,A),PAD​=(A,D).
(72)
The resulting graph subdivision S has vertex set {A,B,C,D,x,y,z} and edges Ax,xB,By,yz,zC,CA,AD. The internal vertex sets are {x},{y,z},∅,∅, so disjointness is explicit. The degrees of vertices of A,B,C,D remain 3,2,2,1, respectively; the three new internal vertices each have degree of a vertex two.
Adding m internal vertices to a finite graph increases both its vertex count and its edge count by m. Here m=3, so four vertices and four edges become seven of each; the graph excess is unchanged. Each replacement graph path remains a route between the same junctions. Thus graph subdivision preserves whether a graph is a planar graph: insert intermediate vertices along a crossing-free drawing, or trace each replacement graph path as one edge to recover a drawing of the original graph. Travel times or capacities are separate modelling choices and are not determined by this adjacency construction.

When the target itself has vertices of degree of a vertex two, adjacency alone need not identify which vertices were original; the specified target mapping supplies that distinction.
